kp.k: Analysis reflects eighteen months of market meetings
kp.d: Andrusko presents the article as a synthesis of lessons from meetings with legal-AI startups and software buyers over the preceding 18 months, not as a market map or formal empirical study. Its claims are therefore framed primarily as investor observations and market judgments rather than measured findings.
qs: I’ll continue with a warning: the below is not a market map.
Instead, I’d like to summarize my key learnings on Legal AI, having met many startups and software buyers focusing on it over the past 18 months.

kp.k: In-house AI use remains narrow and ad hoc
kp.d: The author argues that in-house lawyers commonly use ChatGPT informally for isolated tasks, while deployed specialist products concentrate on document redlining and legal research. He characterizes this as only a small portion of legal work and reports enthusiastic buyer interest without claiming quantified adoption data.
qs: What’s the AI tool in-house lawyers have actually been using the most so far? Arguably, ChatGPT.
In other words, generative AI is often being used ad hoc – a quick contract tweak here, a snippet of research there.
Broadly speaking, the tools that have gained traction so far are confined to things like better document redlining and faster legal research.
Useful, yes, but it’s a fraction of what lawyers do.

kp.k: Point tools face platform and substitution risks
kp.d: Dedicated legal-AI products are said to depend on dominant word-processing and email platforms that are adding their own AI, while low switching costs expose them to replacement. The author also treats general-purpose ChatGPT as a viable, inexpensive competitor for basic legal tasks unless specialist products substantially outperform it.
qs: Platform risk: Unless you own the word processor or email client where lawyers live, you’re stuck integrating into someone else’s platform – and those platforms are quickly rolling out AI features of their own.
Low switching costs: These tools tend to be intuitively useful and quick to show value, but that also makes them easier to replace.
If your shiny new legal AI tool doesn’t dramatically outperform a few well-crafted prompts in ChatGPT, lawyers might shrug and stick to the familiar base case.

kp.k: Cross-organizational collaboration could create legal network effects
kp.d: Using accounting software as analogy, the author argues that legal technology has not yet developed a genuinely multiplayer platform connecting corporate legal departments with outside law firms. He speculates that shared systems could create collaborative value, distribution through professional advisers, and network effects comparable to QuickBooks or Bill.com.
qs: None of these tools are truly multiplayer in the sense of connecting different organizations.
I have yet to see a legal tool optimized for getting law firms and their corporate clients working together in one system.

That collaborative usage delivered real value and even created network effects – accounting firms would recommend the software to their clients, which in turn reinforced the accountants’ own workflows.
Could legal tech achieve a similar dynamic?

kp.k: End-to-end orchestration matters more than isolated automation
kp.d: The author contends that AI redlining and research remain embedded in larger manual processes involving document retrieval, stakeholder communications, approvals, and repositories. He recommends workflow platforms that orchestrate complete sequences of legal work, analogizing the opportunity to Monday.com or Zapier, rather than collections of point solutions.
qs: In other words, today’s AI tools address individual tasks, not the end-to-end process.

If the goal is to actually automate the work, we may need something more akin to a Monday.com or Zapier for legal teams – a platform that orchestrates the entire sequence of legal work – rather than a collection of smart point solutions.
In-house legal departments are clearly eager for AI solutions, but so far they’ve gotten mostly point fixes.

kp.k: Hourly billing can penalize AI-driven efficiency
kp.d: The author uses illustrative BigLaw economics to argue that associate leverage under hourly billing generates substantial partner profit: an associate billing around $700 for roughly 2,000 hours produces about $1.4 million in revenue, costs roughly $500k, and contributes about $900k; at a 4:1 associate-to-partner ratio, this becomes around $3.6 million. On that reasoning, time-saving AI may threaten revenue unless saved capacity can be filled with additional billable work.
qs: At a typical “white shoe” law firm, the average associate might bill around $700 an hour and is expected to rack up roughly 2,000 hours per year.
That yields about $1.4 million in revenue per associate.
Net net, they’re bringing in on the order of $900k in profit for the partner who oversees their work.

With a common associate-to-partner ratio of 4:1, a single partner could be generating around $3.6 million in profit from their team of associates – and true rainmaking partners often leverage even larger teams and drive higher totals.
In plain terms: a time-saving tool that cuts hours out of a law firm’s day isn’t obviously a win for an hourly-billing firm.

kp.k: AI must increase profitable leverage to win firms
kp.d: For hourly firms, the author recommends products that let partners supervise more matters or otherwise increase profit per partner, rather than merely reduce billed time. He treats alignment with the partnership’s associate-leverage model as central to adoption, while qualifying that efficiency can help when a firm is at capacity and can replace saved hours with new work.
qs: If your product can introduce even more leverage into that equation – say, by enabling each partner to handle more matters and generate greater profit per partner – then it will practically sell itself.
Increasing efficiency doesn’t delight a business that makes money by selling time.
Unless that firm is at capacity and can immediately backfill the saved hours with new billable work, you’re asking them to give up revenue.

kp.k: Contingency and fixed-fee work better align incentives
kp.d: Drawing on a16z’s investment thesis for Eve, the author argues that contingency-fee plaintiff firms benefit directly when AI increases case capacity and successful outcomes. He similarly identifies high-volume fixed-fee corporate work as promising because reduced associate time can raise provider margins without changing the client’s set price; these are asserted business-model mechanisms, not quantified outcome findings.
qs: When we invested in Eve, a big part of our thesis was that the plaintiff law model – which operates on contingency fees rather than hourly billing – would be a fertile ground for AI.

In a contingency practice, efficiency directly equals more revenue: an AI that can automate hefty portions of case work means those lawyers can take on many more cases, win more settlements, and ultimately earn far more (since they get a percentage of the outcome).

Likewise, certain high-volume corporate law workflows that are currently flat-fee or fixed-cost could be ripe for AI, because the law firms in those cases are motivated to improve their margins (by using less associate time) while the clients still pay a set price.
In any case, the key is finding a wedge where using AI makes more money for the service provider or doesn’t threaten their revenue.

kp.k: Elite-firm pricing has not yet reset
kp.d: The author reports that the predicted competitive transition from hourly billing toward lower prices, higher volumes, or flat fees has not yet occurred at the top of the market. He attributes this to client willingness to pay premium rates for prestigious counsel in existential matters and predicts that change will require an external force such as client pressure or a new competitor.
qs: In theory, yes – but in reality, we haven’t seen this materialize at the top end of the market yet.
The most prestigious firms are holding the line on the billable hour model, and clients are still willing to pay those rates, especially for high-stakes matters.
When the risks are existential (bet-the-company litigations, critical M&A deals, etc.), clients aren’t clamoring for the cheapest lawyer – they want the best, and they expect to pay accordingly.
Until a true external force (whether client demand or a new competitive entrant) compels a change, elite firms have little incentive to voluntarily slash their hours or rates using AI.

kp.k: Harvey’s brand compensates for limited current usage
kp.d: The author reports that lawyers at firms piloting Harvey are often not using it heavily yet, but argues that Harvey has become a default, low-risk enterprise choice among prestigious firms. In his account, peer adoption, reputation, and fear of missing out produce a compounding brand advantage even without a product-level network effect.
qs: The answer, more often than not, is: “Well, they’re not really using it much… yet.”
It might sound underwhelming – by many accounts, Harvey isn’t (at this stage) deeply embedded in most lawyers’ daily workflows.
In legal AI today, nobody gets fired for buying Harvey.

Each additional white-shoe firm that publicly partners with Harvey makes the next firm that much more likely to jump on board, whether out of FOMO, competitive pressure, or simply the validation that “all our peers are doing it.”

kp.d: The author argues that strict confidentiality and IT controls make bottom-up product-led adoption difficult at major law firms because individual lawyers cannot independently upload sensitive client data. He credits Harvey with pursuing firm-wide agreements involving innovation, IT, knowledge-management, and partner stakeholders, thereby securing availability before widespread end-user adoption.
qs: Harvey recognized early on that a bottoms-up, product-led growth motion would be nearly impossible in the big firm market.

An individual associate or even a partner can’t just start shoving sensitive client data into a new AI tool without the firm’s blessing – not at a reputable firm with strict confidentiality and IT rules.
So Harvey went top-down: from the early days, they sought enterprise-wide agreements with firms, getting buy-in from a coalition of stakeholders.
By landing the whole firm (or a large practice group) in one go, Harvey sidestepped the need to win over end-users one by one at the outset.

kp.k: Confidential data limits cross-client network effects
kp.d: The author argues that legal confidentiality requires client data to remain siloed, preventing vendors from freely training shared models on firms’ interactions and work product. Because competitors can pre-train on the same public legal materials, he concludes that firm-specific fine-tuning may benefit an individual client but is unlikely to create a conventional cross-client data moat under current conditions.
qs: In practice, though, true data network effects in legal are extremely limited by design.

Law firms guard their data like treasure, and rightly so – no firm is going to agree to a vendor using their confidential work product to go train some model that a competitor firm down the street will also use.
So, at least for now, each large client’s data has to remain siloed.
Sure, you can fine-tune on a firm’s internal data to make the product better for that firm, but those gains won’t directly transfer to other clients.
In short, it’s hard to build a traditional data moat or cross-client network effect in this industry under current conditions.

kp.k: Within-client learning may still create product flywheels
kp.d: Using Eve as an example, the author proposes that repeated case work and outcomes can improve intake assessment and case selection within a plaintiff firm, reinforcing product value and customer loyalty. He distinguishes this hypothesized within-client or subvertical feedback loop from a classic network effect and provides no quantified performance evidence.
qs: What is possible, however, are positive feedback loops within a product’s usage at one client, or within a particular subvertical.

For example, it can better assess new case intakes over time – identifying patterns in what makes a case likely to win or settle favorably – and thereby help the firm be smarter about which cases to take on.

While Eve isn’t sharing data across different law firms, it is continuously learning within each firm’s environment and, at a higher level, improving its domain-specific models on patterns that generalize (like how certain fact patterns correlate with outcomes in, say, personal injury cases).
This kind of self-reinforcement can create a competitive edge and strong customer loyalty, even if it’s not a viral user-growth loop like we see in consumer apps.

kp.k: Investment priorities combine incentives, trust, and workflow ownership
kp.d: The author recommends legal-AI companies align ROI with customer pricing models, establish trusted distribution within broad or tightly defined segments, and move beyond isolated features toward collaborative or end-to-end workflows. These are explicitly presented as the principal drivers of a16z’s investment interest rather than neutral market-selection criteria.
qs: The most promising companies deliver clear ROI in the context of their customers’ business model.
They’re not fighting the billable hour – they’re aligned with how users make money (or save it) in a big way.

We’re interested in companies that either have a real shot at becoming the default AI partner for a large segment of the legal market, or are laser-focused on nailing distribution within a single tight-knit subsegment—not just chasing logos.

The most compelling legal AI companies are building products that create positive feedback loops, enable multiplayer collaboration, or own the end-to-end workflow, rather than just inserting an AI feature into an existing task.

kp.k: Transformation depends on incentives and durable platforms
kp.d: The conclusion predicts broader change across in-house departments, law firms, and plaintiff practices, but describes current adoption as an early stage dominated by ad hoc ChatGPT use and point tools. The author argues that lasting platforms will emerge by solving go-to-market barriers, aligning AI with provider economics, and improving through sustained use.
qs: The legal profession is often portrayed as slow to change, but we’re seeing the early signs of a real transformation.

From in-house departments looking to automate grunt work, to law firms exploring how to augment their armies of associates, to plaintiff attorneys scaling up their case loads – everyone knows change is coming.
The base case (ad hoc ChatGPT usage and a few AI point tools) is only the beginning.
The escape velocity will come from cracking the go-to-market code, aligning with incentives, and building products that get better the more people rely on them.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Andrusko describes in-house legal AI adoption as predominantly ad hoc ChatGPT use and narrow task-specific tools, rather than comprehensive automation.
pts.d: As of publication on September 23, 2025, he tentatively identifies ChatGPT as the most-used AI tool among in-house lawyers. He says deployed specialist tools primarily improve redlining and research, leaving most surrounding workflows manual despite strong buyer interest. This is an account of current adoption drawn from his market conversations, not a reported usage survey.

pts.k: Andrusko argues that legal AI point tools face competition from host platforms, easy substitution, and general-purpose ChatGPT.
pts.d: Vendors that do not control lawyers’ word processors or email clients depend on platforms introducing competing AI features. He argues that narrow tools are replaceable when competitors offer slightly better or cheaper performance, and that basic use cases may not warrant specialist software unless it substantially outperforms ChatGPT. These claims concern vendor defensibility and buyer choice, not demonstrated market-share changes.

pts.k: Andrusko proposes cross-organisation collaboration and end-to-end workflow orchestration as opportunities to move legal AI beyond point solutions.
pts.d: He says he has not seen a tool optimised for collaboration between outside firms and their corporate clients. Drawing an analogy with accounting software, he suggests that shared systems could make firms distribution channels and potentially generate network effects. He also proposes orchestration across document retrieval, stakeholder communications, approvals and repositories. These are prospective opportunities framed partly as questions, not established legal-market outcomes.

pts.k: Andrusko argues that hourly billing makes pure time-saving AI commercially unattractive unless it supports additional revenue or greater profit per partner.
pts.d: His mechanism is that reducing billable hours can reduce revenue, whereas tools enabling partners to handle more matters can align with partnership economics. He illustrates the incentive with approximate figures: $700 per associate hour, 2,000 annual hours, $1.4 million revenue, $500,000 salary and bonuses, and a 4:1 associate-to-partner ratio. He describes the resulting amounts as roughly $900,000 profit per associate and $3.6 million per partner’s associate team. These figures are illustrative economic reasoning, not measured effects of AI deployment.

pts.k: Andrusko predicts stronger AI incentives in contingency practices and high-volume fixed-fee work than in conventional hourly practices.
pts.d: For plaintiff-side contingency firms, he argues that automating substantial casework permits more cases, settlements and outcome-linked earnings, with lawyers and clients benefiting from streamlined work and improved chances of success. For certain fixed-fee corporate workflows, reduced associate time could raise provider margins without changing the client’s agreed price. He explicitly links the contingency argument to a16z’s investment thesis for Eve; he provides no quantified outcome study.

pts.k: Andrusko says an AI-driven pricing reset has not yet occurred at the elite end of the market and would require external pressure.
pts.d: He presents competitive fee compression and a shift away from hourly billing as an argument others might make, then qualifies it rather than adopting it as an unconditional prediction. His own account is that prestigious firms continue hourly billing because clients prioritise perceived quality in existential litigation and major transactions. Client demands or a new competitor could change those incentives; no date is specified.

pts.k: Andrusko attributes Harvey’s position to brand, trust and top-down enterprise sales, even where everyday usage remains limited.
pts.d: He reports anecdotal accounts of limited workflow integration while claiming Harvey has become a default AI choice at many prestigious firms. Public firm partnerships supply peer validation that encourages further purchases. Confidentiality and IT restrictions, he argues, make individual-led adoption difficult, favouring agreements supported by innovation, IT, knowledge-management teams and partner champions. He expects firms to retain the platform while anticipating longer-run AI benefits. He distinguishes this brand-based advantage from a product network effect.

pts.k: Andrusko argues that confidentiality limits cross-client data network effects, but within-firm learning and domain-specific feedback can strengthen products.
pts.d: Under current conditions, he says confidential client data must remain siloed, public training sources are broadly shared, and internal fine-tuning benefits do not directly transfer between clients. He contrasts that constraint with Eve’s purported within-firm learning: casework and outcomes can improve intake assessment and case selection. He also describes higher-level improvement from generalisable domain patterns while stating that Eve does not share data between firms. These are qualitative product-mechanism claims without reported performance measurements.

pts.k: Andrusko predicts that durable legal AI platforms will combine incentive alignment, effective distribution, trust and workflow-level value.
pts.d: His concluding investment thesis favours products that create clear customer ROI, become credible default choices or dominate distribution in a focused segment, and extend beyond isolated features. He anticipates transformation through in-house automation, augmentation of law-firm associates and increased plaintiff-firm caseloads, rather than specifying profession-wide job losses or a universal replacement of lawyers.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source primarily offers investor experience, buyer and startup conversations, economic illustrations, product examples and cross-sector analogy.
pts.d: Andrusko grounds the article in 18 months of meetings, not a systematic market map. In-house adoption and Harvey usage claims rely on unspecified conversations and qualitative impressions. The hourly-billing argument uses approximate economics and invokes Cravath-scale compensation data without presenting a dataset. Collaboration opportunities draw on QuickBooks, Sage Intacct and Bill.com as accounting analogies. Eve illustrates a disclosed investment thesis and asserted learning mechanisms. No adoption sample, AI benchmark, controlled productivity study, quantified customer outcome evidence or measured retention data is supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current-state claims concern September 2025; forecasts are conditional and largely undated.
pts.d: The article’s observation window is the preceding 18 months. Qualifiers such as 'arguably', 'yet', 'at this stage' and 'under current conditions' limit claims about ChatGPT prevalence, Harvey usage, pricing persistence and data silos. 'Year one' describes a hypothetical early customer relationship rather than a measured cohort. Future gains depend on replacing saved hours with more work, contingency or fixed-fee incentives, external pressure on elite firms, permission-compatible learning, and successful collaboration or orchestration. No timetable is given for widespread automation, a pricing reset or platform maturity.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted effects differ across corporate buyers, elite hourly firms, contingency firms, fixed-fee practices and AI vendors.
pts.d: In-house lawyers gain task assistance and potentially broader automation and collaboration with outside counsel. Elite-firm partners face revenue and profit incentives that shape adoption, while associates’ work may be augmented or require fewer hours on fixed-fee matters. Plaintiff lawyers may handle more cases and improve intake selection; their clients are described as benefiting from better chances of success and streamlined service. Corporate fixed-fee clients continue paying an agreed price while firms potentially improve margins. Vendors face platform competition and weak switching barriers, but may gain defensibility from reputation, distribution, workflow ownership and within-client learning. The source does not make a specific claim about access to justice or quantify employment displacement.
